metadata.title: Right Format, No Function.
metadata.subtitle: What a Slash Command File Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Teardown-register reading of the reference slash-command file: five fields plus one verbatim ARGUMENTS slot form the interface; the behavior slot is empty by design, and any real function is what you write into it.
metadata.anchor_pair: B05 -> B10 ($ARGUMENTS: planted as the verbatim injection slot, returned to as what still needs code)
metadata.one_flag: B11 (parse-perform-report is the template's chosen shape, not a rule Claude enforces elsewhere)

beats.narration_text: Here's the guess most people make: file in the right folder, right frontmatter, so the command works. It doesn't. What ships is a template — an interface with no behavior wired to it.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('works' -> 'runs a template') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: What you actually want is repeatability: slash, name, maybe a word after it — and Claude does the same specific thing, the same way, every time. That's the design goal.

production_viz.label: THE SHORTCUT
production_viz.caption: type it once, get it every time

beats.narration_text: Here's what's easy to assume: file exists, frontmatter parses, name is right — so the command already does something. That guess treats the frontmatter as the command. It isn't. It's the declaration of one.

Run the reference example that ships with Claude's plugins — here's what actually comes back. A plain template describing three phases: parse, perform, report. No folder created. No file touched. The action slot is there. Nothing was written into it.

production_viz.label: RUN IT
production_viz.caption: a template comes back — no action taken

beats.narration_text: Underneath, the file is five pieces of setup — name, description, argument-hint, allowed-tools, model — one YAML block at the top. They pre-declare metadata; none of them decide what happens next.

production_viz.label: FIVE FIELDS
production_viz.caption: one block of setup at the top of the file

beats.narration_text: Here's the one that matters most: whatever you type after the command lands, word for word, in a single named slot inside the file — ARGUMENTS. Type slash-greet Nik, and the literal string Nik appears there. No parsing, no interpretation — string substitution, verbatim.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — $ARGUMENTS
production_viz.caption: THE ANCHOR — remember this: verbatim, every time

beats.narration_text: Argument-hint is what a user sees before typing anything — the reminder text next to the command's name, showing the shape of input expected. It's help text. It doesn't validate what gets typed. Menu hint, not schema.

production_viz.label: ARGUMENT-HINT
production_viz.caption: the hint text before you've typed anything

beats.narration_text: Allowed-tools does something different: it pre-approves a specific list of tools for this one command, so Claude runs them without asking each time. Scope is per-command, not global — a friction cut here, permission expansion nowhere else.

Model lets this one command run on a different model than your default conversation — a cheap fast one for something simple, a stronger one when the reasoning matters. Per-invocation override, not a session change.

production_viz.label: MODEL OVERRIDE
production_viz.caption: a different model, just for this command

beats.narration_text: The body of the file follows the same three-step shape: parse whatever arrived in ARGUMENTS, perform the actual work, report back what happened. In the reference file, that shape is described in prose — the outline. Nothing on the outline runs code.

Back to ARGUMENTS: type slash-greet Nik, and Nik really does arrive, letter for letter, right where the file said it would. The substitution runs. What doesn't run is anything using it — that part is the function, and the function is what you still write yourself.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS
production_viz.caption: it lands exactly as typed — using it is still yours to write

beats.narration_text: One flag: parse-perform-report is this file's chosen shape, not something Claude enforces elsewhere. The layout has an older sibling too — a single file, commands slash name dot m d — which loads the same way. Same contract, different folder. The three phases are this template's convention, not the plugin system's rule.

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG — TWO LAYOUTS
production_viz.caption: loads the same either way — this shape is the template's choice

beats.narration_text: Matching the format perfectly doesn't prove the command does anything real. The reference file matches it exactly, and running it still returns the template — shape right, behavior slot empty. That's the whole point of the split.

production_viz.label: FORMAT, NOT FUNCTION
production_viz.caption: matching the format doesn't prove it does anything

beats.narration_text: Skipping an optional field doesn't mean it's broken either. Leave out argument-hint and the command still runs — users just don't see that reminder before they type. Optional means the parser tolerates its absence, not that dropping it kills the command.

production_viz.label: OPTIONAL, NOT BROKEN
production_viz.caption: skip an optional field, and it still runs

beats.narration_text: Five fields and one slot called ARGUMENTS are the scaffold of a slash command — that's the interface. Matching the format gets you the shape. What happens when someone actually runs it is the function, and the function is still yours to write.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to build a real slash command called slash word-count. It should take a file path as its required argument, count the words in that file, and report the total back to me. Show me the exact SKILL.md file you'd write for it, and explain — in plain terms — what ARGUMENTS actually contains the moment I run the command. Go deeper: ask it to compare putting the counting logic inside SKILL.md as prose instructions versus calling out to a small script — which one is easier to change later, and which one is easier for Claude to get right the first time?
